L23@P1: for Future Research

L25@P1: Stochastic Model
L26@P1: Predictive Control
L27@P1: Model predictive control (MPC) has demonstrated exceptional success for the high-performance control of complex systems [1], [2].
L28@P1: The conceptual simplicity of MPC as well as
L29@P1: its ability to effectively cope with the complex
L30@P1: dynamics of systems with multiple inputs and outputs, input and state/output constraints, and conflicting control
L31@P1: objectives have made it an attractive multivariable constrained control approach [1]. MPC (a.k.a. receding-horizon
L32@P1: control) solves an open-loop constrained optimal control
L33@P1: problem (OCP) repeatedly in a receding-horizon manner
L34@P1: [3]. The OCP is solved over a finite sequence of control actions {, uu 01,, f uN- 1} at every sampling time instant that the
L35@P1: current state of the system is measured. The first element
L36@P1: of the sequence of optimal control actions is applied to the
L37@P1: system, and the computations are then repeated at the next
L38@P1: sampling time. Thus, MPC replaces a feedback control law
L39@P1: r()$ , which can have formidable offline computation, with
L40@P1: the repeated solution of an open-loop OCP [2]. In fact, repeated solution of the OCP
L41@P1: confers an “implicit” feedback action to MPC to cope
L42@P1: with system uncertainties
L43@P1: and disturbances. Alternatively, explicit MPC approaches
L44@P1: circumvent the need to solve an
L45@P1: OCP online by deriving relationships
L46@P1: for the optimal control actions in terms of an “explicit”
L47@P1: function of the state and reference vectors. However, explicit MPC is not typically intended to replace standard MPC
L48@P1: but, rather, to extend its area of application [4]–[6].
L49@P1: Although MPC offers a certain degree of robustness to
L50@P1: system uncertainties due to its receding-horizon implementation, its deterministic formulation typically renders
L51@P1: it inherently inadequate for systematically dealing with
L52@P1: uncertainties. Addressing the general OCP for uncertain systems would involve solving the dynamic programming (DP)
L53@P1: problem over (arbitrary) feedback control laws r()$ [7], [8].
L54@P1: Solving the DP problem, however, is deemed to be impractical for real-world control applications since computational
L55@P1: complexity of a DP problem increases exponentially with
L56@P1-2: image licensed by ingram publishingDECEMBER 2016 « IEEE CONTROL SYSTEMS MAGAZINE 31
L57@P2: uncertainties and their interactions with the system
L58@P2: dynamics, constraints, and performance criteria. Parameterized feedback control laws allow for using the knowledge of predicted uncertainties in computing
L59@P2: the control law, while reducing the computations to poly nom ial dependence on t he
L60@P2: state dimension [16].
L61@P2: RMPC approaches rely on bounded, deterministic descriptions of system uncertainties.
L62@P2: In real-world systems, however, uncertainties
L63@P2: are often considered to be of probabilistic nature.
L64@P2: When the stochastic system uncertainties can be
L65@P2: adequately characterized, it is more natural to explicitly
L66@P2: account for the probabilistic occurrence of uncertainties in a
L67@P2: control design method. Hence, stochastic MPC (SMPC) has
L68@P2: recently emerged with the aim of systematically incorporating the probabilistic descriptions of uncertainties into a
L69@P2: stochastic OCP. In particular, SMPC exploits the probabilistic uncertainty descriptions to define chance constraints,
L70@P2: which require the state/output constraints be satisfied
L71@P2: with at least a priori specified probability level—or, alternatively, be satisfied in expectation (see, for example, [17]–
L72@P2: [20], and the references therein for
L73@P2: various approaches to chance-constrained optimization). Chance
L74@P2: constraints enable the systematic use of the stochastic characterization of uncertainties
L75@P2: to allow for an admissible level
L76@P2: of closed-loop constraint violation in a probabilistic sense.
L77@P2: SMPC allows for systematically seeking tradeoffs between
L78@P2: fulfilling the control objectives
L79@P2: and guaranteeing a probabilistic constraint satisfaction due to uncertainty. The ability to effectively handle constraints in a stochastic setting is
L80@P2: particularly important for MPC of uncertain systems when
L81@P2: high-performance operation is realized in the vicinity of
L82@P2: constraints. In addition, the probabilistic framework of
L83@P2: SMPC enables shaping the probability distribution of
L84@P2: system states/outputs. The ability to regulate the probability distribution of system states/outputs is important for
L85@P2: the safe and economic operation of complex systems when
L86@P2: the control cost function is asymmetric, that is, when the
L87@P2: probability distributions have long tails [21].
L88@P2: Stochastic optimal control is rooted in stochastic programming and chance-constrained optimization; see, for
L89@P2: example, [22] and [23] for a historical perspective. The pioneering work on chance-constrained MPC includes [17],
L90@P2: [18], [24], and [25]. In recent years, interest in SMPC has
L91@P2: been growing from both the theoretical and application
L92@P2: standpoints. SMPC has found applications in many different areas, including building climate control, power
L93@P2: the state dimension (known as curse of
L94@P2: dimensionality) [9].
L95@P2: The past two decades have witnessed
L96@P2: significant developments in the area of robust
L97@P2: MPC (RMPC) with the aim to devise computationally
L98@P2: affordable optimal control approaches that allow for the
L99@P2: systematic handling of system uncertainties. RMPC
L100@P2: approaches consider set-membership-type uncertainties—uncertainties are assumed to be deterministic and
L101@P2: lie in a bounded set. Early work on RMPC was primarily
L102@P2: based on min–max OCP formulations, where the control
L103@P2: actions are designed with respect to worst-case evaluations of the cost function and the constraints of the OCP
L104@P2: must be satisfied for all possible uncertainty realizations
L105@P2: (see, for example, [10] and [11]). Min–max MPC approaches
L106@P2: could not, however, contain the “spread” of state trajectories, rendering the optimal control actions overly conservative or, possibly, infeasible [12]. To address the
L107@P2: shortcomings of min–max OCPs, tube-based MPC has
L108@P2: recently been developed [12]–[15]. Tube-based MPC
L109@P2: approaches use a partially separable feedback control law
L110@P2-3: parameterization to allow for the direct handling of 32 IEEE CONTROL SYSTEMS MAGAZINE » DECEMBER 2016
L111@P3: generation and distribution, chemical processes, operation
L112@P3: research, networked controlled systems, and vehicle path
L113@P3: planning. Table 1 provides an overview of various emerging application areas for SMPC; this table by no means provides an exhaustive list of SMPC applications reported in
L114@P3: the literature. The majority of reported SMPC approaches
L115@P3: have been developed for linear systems (for example, algorithms based on the stochastic tube [26] or affine parameterization of control policy [27]). Several SMPC applications
L116@P3: to linear and nonlinear systems have been reported based
L117@P3: on stochastic programming-based approaches [28]–[30]
L118@P3: and Monte Carlo sampling techniques [31], [32]. Stochastic
L119@P3: nonlinear MPC (SNMPC) has received relatively little
L120@P3: attention, with only a few applications reported mainly in
L121@P3: the area of process control [33]–[35].
L122@P3: This article gives an overview of the main developments
L123@P3: in the area of SMPC in the past decade and provides the
L124@P3: reader with an impression of the different SMPC algorithms
L125@P3: and the key theoretical challenges in stochastic predictive
L126@P3: control without undue mathematical complexity. The general formulation of a stochastic OCP is first presented, followed by an overview of SMPC approaches for linear and
L127@P3: nonlinear systems. Suggestions of some avenues for future
L128@P3: research in this rapidly evolving field concludes the article.

L325@P4: The key challenges in solving the stochastic OCP (6)
L326@P4: include 1) the arbitrary form of the feedback control laws
L327@P4: ri()$ , 2) the nonconvexity and general intractability of
L328@P4: chance constraints [40], [41], and 3) the computational
L329@P4: complexity associated with uncertainty propagation
L330@P4: through complex system dynamics (for example, nonlinear systems). In addition, establishing theoretical properties, such as recursive feasibility and stability, of the
L331@P4: stochastic OCP (6) poses a major challenge. Numerous
L332@P4: SMPC approaches have been developed to obtain tractable surrogates for the stochastic OCP (6). Table 2 summarizes the key features based on which SMPC approaches
L333@P4: can be broadly categorized. In subsequent sections, various SMPC formulations will be analyzed in light of the
L334@P4: distinguishing features given in Table 2. Broadly, SMPC
L335@P4: approaches can be categorized in terms of the type of
L336@P4: system dynamics, that is, linear or nonlinear dynamics.
L337@P4: SMPC approaches for linear systems are further categorized based on three main schools of thought: stochastictube approaches [42]–[46], approaches using affine
L338@P4: parameterization of the control policy [47]–[56], and stochastic programming-based approaches [56]–[62]. There
L339@P4: has been much less development in the area of SMPC for
L340@P4: nonlinear systems. The main contributions in this area
L341@P4: can be categorized in terms of their underlying uncertainty propagation methods, namely sample-based
L342@P4: approaches [31], [32], [63], Gaussian-mixture approximations [64], generalized polynomial chaos (gPC) [33], [34],
L343@P4: [65], and the Fokker–Planck equation [35], [66], [67]. It is
L344@P4: worth nothing, however, that a unique way to classify the
L345@P4: numerous SMPC approaches reported in the literature
L346@P4: does not exist. It has been attempted throughout the discussion to contrast the various SMPC approaches in
L347@P4: terms of the key features listed in Table 2.
